name: Smithsonite
toxicityNote: A zinc carbonate that may contain trace cadmium or copper; do not ingest or make elixirs, and avoid dust.
spiritual: Helps with letting go of tension
physical: Traditionally associated with comfort during stressful times
Crystal healers link it to relaxation of the digestive area
Folklore connects it with general vitality
Often kept near for gentle calm
summary: Smithsonite is a pastel zinc carbonate in blues, pinks and greens, treasured as a soothing stone of peace, nurturing and gentle emotional healing.
intro: Smithsonite arrives in the softest palette of any mineral in the shop, from lavender to pink, mint, honey and a sea-glass blue. It often forms in rounded, botryoidal masses with a pearly sheen, like frozen candy floss or wax. Zinc carbonate in the oxidised zone of zinc deposits is what builds it, and the colours come from trace copper, cadmium, cobalt and manganese. Cut cabochons and polished slabs show gentle banding and a smooth glow. Fine blue-green pieces from Mexico and the old Kelly mine in New Mexico are especially admired by collectors.
history: Smithsonite is named for James Smithson, the English chemist and mineralogist who recognised in 1802 that this zinc carbonate was distinct from the zinc silicate hemimorphite, with which it had long been muddled under the name calamine. Smithson's bequest later founded the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, DC. As an ore, it was mined for zinc and used in brass making since antiquity. Gem-quality pastel varieties became popular in the twentieth century, with specimens from Tsumeb in Namibia, Lavrion in Greece and Mexico becoming collector favourites.
meaning: Smithsonite is associated with nurturing, peace and gentle emotional healing. In the crystal tradition, its soft pastels are linked to the heart and throat, helping people express tenderness and receive support. Practitioners use it for self-care routines, for soothing emotional overwhelm, and for easing fear of conflict. It is sometimes called a stone of the inner child, bringing a feeling of safety and comfort. Pink smithsonite is said to encourage loving relationships, blue to support calm speech, and green to help with emotional renewal. It is a quiet stone for quiet days, suited to those who respond better to softness than intensity.
howToUse: Keep a palm-sized piece by your bed or sofa as part of an evening wind-down. Hold it over your heart for a few slow breaths after a stressful day. Carry a small tumble in your pocket for steady comfort at work. Place pink or peach pieces in a relationship space, and blue in a place of conversation or study. Use it in a self-care grid with rose quartz and selenite. Jewellery is possible but fragile, so choose pendants and earrings rather than rings.
care: Smithsonite is a carbonate, so it is sensitive to acids and can lose its polish if soaked. Avoid water, vinegar and cleaning products. Wipe with a soft dry cloth. Cleanse by smoke, sound or selenite, and charge under gentle moonlight. Strong sun can fade pastel colours, so keep it in shade. Store it separately in a soft pouch since it scratches easily. Do not use for elixirs, and wash your hands after handling raw pieces.
identify: Genuine smithsonite shows waxy-pearly botryoidal surfaces, fine banding and natural soft pastels. Dyed calcite, chalcedony and glass are frequent fakes, often with unnaturally saturated colour. A drop of dilute acid will fizz on real smithsonite, but do not test valuable pieces. Hemimorphite and chrysoprase can look similar. Because it is heavier than calcite, real specimens feel dense for their size. Choose reputable sellers who state the locality.

faq.a: In crystal tradition, smithsonite is a gentle stone for emotional comfort, nurturing and inner peace. People keep it near for calm and tenderness. These are metaphysical beliefs, not medical claims.
Avoid it. As a carbonate, smithsonite is soft and sensitive to acids and moisture, which can dull the surface. Wipe with a dry cloth and cleanse with smoke, sound or selenite.
